transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been going on that made you decide to come see me?

Well, hi, Dr. [Name]. I, uh... I guess I'm here because things at work are just... they're really coming to a head. I do general maintenance and repair, you know, fixing a bit of everything, and I've been doing it a long time. But lately—well, maybe not just lately, but it's gotten so bad now—I keep forgetting things. Important things. Like, I'll have scheduled callbacks to check on a repair, or specific work orders that come through, and they just... poof. Gone from my mind. And it’s not just the big stuff either, it’s even basic follow-ups I promised people. Like, I’ll tell someone in accounting I’ll go look at their squeaky chair after lunch, and then three days later they’re asking me about it and I have zero memory of ever having that conversation. It’s embarrassing, honestly. It’s piled up so much that my supervisor actually pulled me aside. I’ve been up for a promotion, you know, a chance to move up and maybe not be crawling under sinks quite as much, but they basically sent me here because if I can't get this under control, I'm going to lose my shot at it. And I really need this promotion, I've worked hard, but my brain just won't hold onto these schedules and promises no matter how much I try to remind myself.
When did you first start noticing these memory problems? Was it something that happened suddenly, or has it been gradually getting worse over time?

Well, it’s... I mean, looking back, I guess I've always been a little bit of a scatterbrain, but as far as it being this severe? It really, really took a nosedive about 11 months ago. That's when everything just went completely off the rails for me. 

See, what happened was, this new management company took over our building contracts—which was a whole big chaotic mess on its own, let me tell you, everybody was sweating bullets about their jobs and if they were going to clean house—but anyway, they came in and completely gutted how we do our day-to-day operations. We used to just have these little paper work tickets, right? I'd fold them up, stick 'em in my shirt pocket, and I always had them right there to look at. 

But about 11 months ago, they switched our entire department over to digital work orders. They handed us all these tablets. And the documentation they expect now... it is so strict, doctor. It's ridiculous. You have to log the exact minute you start, the exact minute you stop, type out these long descriptions of the parts you used... and if I set that tablet down while I'm, you know, elbow-deep fixing a garbage disposal, by the time I wipe my hands off, the screen is locked and my mind is just completely blank on what I was supposed to log or who I was supposed to follow up with. It's just gone. So, yeah, it wasn't really a gradual thing recently, it was noticeably worse, like hitting a sudden brick wall right around 11 months back when they brought in the new management and all those digital systems and strict rules.
Outside of work—at home, with family, doing hobbies—have you noticed these same memory problems, or is it mainly just happening at work with the tablets and work orders?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my sister about this over the weekend. We were at her place for a barbecue—she always does these big family get-togethers for Labor Day, though this year it rained so we were all crammed in her kitchen, which is tiny, by the way—but anyway, I was telling her how much I'm struggling at work, and she asked me the exact same thing. And honestly, I don't really know. 

I mean, I don't *think* it's happening as much at home? But my home life is pretty routine, you know? It's just me and my dog, Buster—he's a beagle mix, sweetest thing, but stubborn as a mule—and we kind of just have our set schedule. I wake up, I feed him, I go to work, I come home, I make dinner, we watch TV. There aren't really... I don't have a tablet at home buzzing at me to log my time or follow up with Mrs. Henderson in apartment 4B about her leaky faucet, right? 

But then again, maybe I am forgetting things and I just don't have a supervisor breathing down my neck to point it out. Like, last week, I went to the grocery store to get milk, and I came back with dog food, paper towels, and a rotisserie chicken, but no milk. And I stood there in the kitchen just staring at the bags, trying to figure out how I managed that. But is that the same thing as the work stuff? Or is that just, you know, being 49 and tired after a long day of crawling under sinks? I really couldn't tell you for sure, doctor. It just feels so much more... heavy at work, because the stakes are so high with this promotion. At home, if I forget the milk, I just drink my coffee black, you know? It's annoying, but it's not going to cost me my job. So, I don't know. I'm really not sure if it's the exact same problem or just regular everyday forgetting.

When you're relaxed at home—say, watching TV with Buster in the evening—can you remember things pretty well, like what happened during the day or conversations you had? Or do you find yourself struggling to recall things even when there's no work stress or pressure?

Well, that's a good question, doctor, and it's something I've actually sat and thought about quite a bit. You know, when I'm sitting there in my recliner—it's this old brown leather thing, probably needs replacing, but it's so comfortable—and Buster is curled up on my feet, snoring away... I mean, I *feel* relaxed. The TV is on, maybe I'm watching one of those home renovation shows, which is ironic given what I do all day, but I just like seeing things get fixed without me having to do the heavy lifting, you know? 

But as for remembering things... I honestly don't know. Like, if you asked me right now what I watched on TV three nights ago, I couldn't tell you to save my life. But is that because my memory is bad, or is it because those shows all just blend together after a while? It's the same formula every time: they find black mold, they cry about the budget, and then it all looks beautiful at the end. I don't really *need* to remember it. 

And as for conversations... well, it's just me and Buster, so I'm not really having deep conversations at home. I talk to him, sure, but he doesn't talk back, unless he thinks it's dinner time. If I talk to my sister on the phone... I mean, I think I remember the gist of what we say? She talks a mile a minute, mostly about her kids—my niece just started high school and it's all drama, drama, drama—so I mostly just listen and say "uh-huh" at the right times. If she asked me the next day to repeat exactly what she said, I'd probably struggle. But again, is that this memory problem, or is it just that I was half-asleep in my chair while she was venting? 

So, I really don't know. It's not like at work where there's a clear "you forgot to log this part" or "you missed this appointment." At home, the pressure is off, so if I forget something, it just... evaporates. I don't even realize I've forgotten it because there's no consequence. I just don't have a good answer for you on that one, doctor. It's all just kind of a blur once I clock out and get home.

You mentioned forgetting the milk at the grocery store last week. When you're doing things like that—routine tasks at home or errands—do you find yourself getting confused about what you're doing, or do you just forget what you went there for in the first place?

Oh, no, no, I wouldn't say I'm confused. It's not like I'm wandering the aisles of the grocery store not knowing who I am or how I got there, you know? I know exactly what I'm doing. I'm looking at the endcaps, I'm picking out Buster's dog food, I'm grabbing that rotisserie chicken because they always have them fresh out of the roaster right around 5:30 when I get off shift, and they smell amazing. I just... completely, one hundred percent forget the original reason I walked through the automatic doors. The milk just ceases to exist in my brain until I'm standing in my kitchen. 

But see, forgetting the milk, that's just... whatever. It's a minor annoyance. What really brought me in here today, the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair talking to you, isn't the grocery store. It's that this exact same kind of forgetting is happening with my job, but the stakes are real. I keep forgetting these scheduled callbacks I'm supposed to make. Like, a tenant will have a clanking radiator, and I'll say, "I'll come back at 3:00 with the bleed key," and I just... don't. I completely forget the digital work orders on that new tablet they gave us. I forget even the most basic follow-ups I promised people right to their faces. I'll look a nice lady in the eye, promise I'll come back with a new hinge for her cabinet, and the second I turn the corner and head down the hallway, the thought is just gone. Wiped clean.

And it’s just... it's piled up so much now, doctor. Just this massive mountain of missed orders and angry tenants calling the front office to complain about me, which they never used to do! It got so bad that my supervisor, Dave—who is usually a pretty laid-back guy, we've worked together for six years—he had to pull me into the back office last week. He basically told me that work is sending me here to get evaluated because of all these dropped balls. Because, like I mentioned, I'm up for this promotion to Senior Tech. It's a really big deal for me. It means better pay, regular hours, no more on-call weekends crawling under sinks at 2 AM. But Dave told me flat out that I am going to lose my shot at moving up if I don't get this sorted out immediately. 

So, to answer your question, no, I'm not confused at all about what I'm doing. I'm just forgetting everything I'm supposed to do, and it's piled up so high it's about to cost me my career.

Besides the memory issues, have you noticed any other changes—like feeling confused about where you are or what time it is, having trouble finding words, or feeling unusually anxious or worried most days?

Well, let me think about that. Confused about where I am? Oh, gosh, no, definitely nothing like that. I mean, I've worked at the same apartment complex for six years now. I know every single inch of that place. I know every boiler room, every crawlspace, every shortcut through the courtyard. Honestly, if you blindfolded me and dropped me in the middle of Building C, I could probably tell you exactly where I was just by the smell of Mrs. Gable's cabbage soup—she makes it every Tuesday, bless her heart, and it just permeates the whole floor. So no, I always know exactly where I am. 

And as for what time it is, well, my dog Buster is basically a furry alarm clock. He has this internal radar that goes off at exactly 5:00 AM for his morning walk and 5:30 PM for his dinner, and he will literally sit there and whine at me if I'm even two minutes late. Plus, in my line of work, you're always looking at the clock, trying to figure out if you have enough time to snake a drain before your lunch break or if you should just wait until after. So time is never really a mystery to me.

Trouble finding words? No, I don't think so. My sister would probably tell you I have the exact opposite problem! I can talk your ear off once I get going, especially if it's a story about one of my crazy tenants. I never forget the names of my tools, either. A basin wrench is a basin wrench, a Phillips head is a Phillips head. I never find myself standing there holding a wrench and not knowing what to call it. The words are all there just fine. 

And as for feeling unusually anxious or worried... I mean, I'm stressed right now, sure. But I think anyone would be, right? Dave pulling me into the office and telling me I might lose this promotion to Senior Tech—that really put the fear of God in me, because I need that pay bump. My truck needs a new transmission, and that's not cheap. So yes, I'm worried about my job, and I get a knot in my stomach when I realize I forgot another work order. But it's not like I'm just sitting around my house biting my nails over nothing, you know? It's a very specific, logical stress about the fact that I keep dropping the ball at work. If I could just figure out how to keep those digital work orders in my head and actually show up when I promise I will, I'd be right as rain. So it really is just the forgetting. That's the only thing that's really out of whack.

You mentioned things got much worse about 11 months ago when the new management came in. Around that same time, did you have any head injuries, falls, accidents, or any kind of illness or medical event—like a high fever, infection, or anything that required you to see a doctor?

Head injuries? Oh, gosh, no, nothing like that. I mean, sure, I bump my head on a low-hanging pipe in the boiler room every now and then—comes with the territory when you're working in tight spaces—but never anything serious. No concussions, no falling off ladders, no hospital trips. And I haven't been sick either. No high fevers or anything. Honestly, I can't even remember the last time I took a sick day. I've got a pretty strong immune system, I guess. 

No, the reason I brought up the 11-month mark isn't because of anything medical happening to my body. It’s just that things have been noticeably worse for about 11 months because that's exactly when the new management company took over and completely changed our department over to digital work orders and much stricter documentation. 

Before they came in, things were so simple. Dave would just hand me a yellow carbon-copy paper ticket, I’d fold it up, stick it right here in my front shirt pocket, go fix the leaky faucet or whatever it was, and then I’d just hand the ticket back to him at the end of the day. It was physical, you know? I could feel it in my pocket. But 11 months ago, these new corporate folks came in and decided we needed to be "modernized." They took away our paper tickets and gave us all these tablets—they're in these thick, heavy black rubber cases so we don't shatter the screens if we drop them on the concrete—and they instituted all this incredibly strict documentation. 

Now, instead of just fixing a problem, I have to pull out the tablet, log into the app—which logs me out every twenty minutes, by the way, which is incredibly frustrating—click 'start job', take a 'before' picture, type out every single thing I'm doing, log the exact part numbers of the materials I used, take an 'after' picture, and then have the tenant sign it with their finger. And if I get a call on my radio right in the middle of doing all that, or if Mrs. Gable starts talking to me about her grandkids while I'm trying to type, I just completely lose my place. I'll put the tablet down to answer the radio, and then I just walk away and forget to finish the digital ticket. Or I'll promise to come back with a part, but because I haven't written it down on a physical piece of paper, it just vanishes from my mind. 

So, no, no accidents or fevers or anything like that. It's just that for the last 11 months, this new digital system and all this strict tracking they want... it's like it requires a completely different part of my brain, and that part just isn't working right.

Over these past 11 months, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling down, sad, or hopeless? Or have you lost interest in things you normally enjoy, like those home renovation shows or spending time with Buster?

Down or sad? Hopeless? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, sure, I'm frustrated, like I was saying about Dave and the tablet and all that mess, because it's just so aggravating to know you can do the physical labor but the digital stuff trips you up. But sad? No. I still wake up in a pretty good mood most days, ready to get to work. 

And as for losing interest in things... oh, definitely not. Are you kidding? Buster is my absolute best friend. We still do our exact same routine. In fact, just yesterday after work, even though I was completely exhausted from dealing with a backed-up sewer line in Building B—which, let me tell you, was a total nightmare because the oak tree roots had gotten into the main pipe and I had to snake the whole entire thing—anyway, I still took Buster out to the dog park for a solid hour. He loves chasing those little orange rubber balls, the ones that bounce really high, and he goes absolutely nuts for them. I could never get tired of watching him run around like a goofball. It really clears my head after a long shift.

And the home renovation shows? Oh, I am still completely obsessed. I watch them every single night while I eat my dinner. I actually just started a new season of this one show where they buy these total disaster houses sight unseen, and the plumbing in them is always a complete wreck. I sit there yelling at the TV, telling the guys they are doing it all wrong, pointing out that a certain valve is going to leak in a year, or asking why they are using PVC when they should be using copper. It is actually kind of hilarious because I do this stuff all day long for a living, and yet I come home and watch other people do it on television. You would think I would be sick of it, but I just love it. 

So, yeah, I still love all my normal stuff. I am not down or hopeless or anything like that. I just really need to figure out how to keep those work orders in my brain before Dave decides he has had enough of me.

When you're doing a repair job that you've done many times before—like fixing a leaky faucet or bleeding a radiator, something routine that you know how to do—do you have trouble remembering the steps of how to do it, or do you remember how to do the actual work itself just fine?

Oh, the actual work? No, no, not at all. I remember how to do all of that just fine. It's really like muscle memory at this point, you know? I mean, take a leaky faucet, for example, since you mentioned it. Most of the units in our complex still have these older single-handle faucets—the ones with the little ball assembly inside? I must have rebuilt a thousand of those over the last six years. I don't even have to think about the steps anymore. I know exactly what to do. 

First, obviously, I get under the sink and shut off the hot and cold supply lines—which, let me tell you, half the time those shut-off valves are completely stuck because nobody ever turns them, so I always have to bring my channel locks just to get them to budge. But once the water is off, I just take my Allen wrench, pop off the handle, unscrew the dome cap—sometimes you need a pair of pliers for that if there's hard water buildup, which we have a lot of in this city, it just ruins the fixtures—and then I just pull out the cam and the little rubber seats and springs. Swap in the new ones, put it all back together, and turn the water back on. 

I can do the whole thing in under ten minutes, easy. My hands just know exactly where to go and what tool to grab from my belt next. Same thing with bleeding a radiator or swapping out a garbage disposal or replacing a wax ring on a toilet. The steps are all right there in my head, perfectly clear. I never, ever stand there staring at a pipe wondering what to do next. The physical work is honestly the easiest part of my day! 

Like I was saying before, the problem isn't the doing. The doing is fine. It's just... it's the remembering to actually go to the apartment to do it in the first place. Or remembering to type all those little steps I just told you into that heavy black tablet before I walk out the door. If Dave just pointed at a broken sink and said 'fix it,' I'd have it done perfectly every single time. So, no, I definitely don't forget how to do the repairs themselves. My brain is perfectly fine when my hands are working.

Before the new management company came in 11 months ago and things changed at work, did you ever notice any memory problems at all—even small ones—or did the memory issues only start after that stressful change happened?

Well, if I really sit down and think about it... no, it definitely didn't just start 11 months ago. I mean, the 11 months is just when it became a massive problem for my paycheck, you know, because of those tablets and the new rules. But honestly? I remember being exactly like this way, way back in grade school, long before I ever had to worry about job pressure or corporate management breathing down my neck. 

I can still picture my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—wait, no, Mrs. Gable is the tenant in 4B who always talks about her grandkids. Mrs. *Garrison*. That was her name. Anyway, she used to tell my parents at every single parent-teacher conference that I was a really bright kid, that I had all this potential, but... well, there was always a 'but.' And the 'but' was always that I was constantly misplacing my papers. I would actually do the homework, I swear I would, and then it would just vanish into the absolute black hole of my desk or the bottom of my backpack. 

And it wasn't just losing things, either. If she gave us a list of instructions for a project, I would completely miss parts of the directions. Like, she’d say to read a chapter, answer the odd questions, and draw a diagram, and I'd only hear the first part and just stop there. I always, always needed her to come over and give me reminders to actually finish my classwork. I'd be staring out the window watching the school custodian fix the chain on the swing set—which is probably why I do what I do now, honestly, I was always fascinated by how things went together—and she'd have to physically tap on my desk to get me to finish my spelling sheet. 

So, yeah, it’s not a new thing at all. The old paper ticket system at work, it just sort of... worked with my brain, I guess, because I could shove the ticket in my pocket and it was a physical reminder that I could touch. But now that everything is invisible and floating around on a screen, it's just exactly like being back in Mrs. Garrison's class, losing my papers and missing the directions all over again.

When you were in school and even as a young adult before this job, did people ever tell you that you had trouble paying attention or staying focused on things, or was it mainly just about losing papers and forgetting instructions?

Oh, absolutely. It was definitely about paying attention, too, not just the lost papers. My mom used to joke—well, she wasn't really joking, she was usually pretty fed up—that I was always off in the clouds. My report cards always had those little checkmarks next to "easily distracted" or "has trouble staying on task." 

And it followed me right into being a young adult, too. When I was in my twenties, I worked at this local hardware store over on 4th Street—it's gone now, got bought out by one of the big box places years ago, which is a shame because they had the best fastener aisle in the city—but my manager there, Rick, he was always snapping his fingers at me. I'd be supposed to be taking inventory of the brass fittings or reading a memo from the supplier, and I'd just completely zone out. I'd be watching a customer try to figure out the key-cutting machine, or listening to the hum of the overhead lights, and I just couldn't keep my focus locked on what was right in front of me. 

And honestly, it's the exact same feeling I get now at work with this new system. It's just this inability to stay locked onto something if I'm just reading it instead of doing it. Like, I can start a digital work order thinking I’ve got it, but halfway through reading the notes my mind slips off to the next noise or job and I realize I don’t know what I just looked at. I'll hear a dog barking three floors down, or a truck backing up in the alley, or I'll start thinking about a drywall patch I need to sand in unit 2C, and suddenly I'm just staring at this heavy black tablet like it's written in a foreign language. I have to read the exact same sentence three or four times because my focus just completely evaporates. 

So, yeah, people have been telling me I have trouble paying attention my whole entire life. If I have to just sit and sustain my focus on words or instructions, whether it was a textbook back in the day or Dave's digital tickets now, my brain just... goes on vacation.

I can do the whole thing in under ten minutes, easy. My hands just know exactly where to go and what tool to grab from my belt next. doctor.question: When you were in school and even as a young adult before this job, did people ever tell you that you had trouble paying attention or staying focused on things, or was it mainly just about losing papers and forgetting instructions?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I can start a digital work order thinking I’ve got it, but halfway through reading the notes my mind slips off to the next noise or job and I realize I don’t know what I just looked at.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I had trouble paying attention or staying focused on things in the past, which maps to difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It was definitely about paying attention, too, not just the lost papers. My mom used to joke—well, she wasn't really joking, she was usually pretty fed up—that I was always off in the clouds. My report cards always had those little checkmarks next to "easily distracted" or "has trouble staying on task." 

And it followed me right into being a young adult, too. When I was in my twenties, I worked at this local hardware store over on 4th Street—it's gone now, got bought out by one of the big box places years ago, which is a shame because they had the best fastener aisle in the city—but my manager there, Rick, he was always snapping his fingers at me. I'd be supposed to be taking inventory of the brass fittings or reading a memo from the supplier, and I'd just completely zone out. I'd be watching a customer try to figure out the key-cutting machine, or listening to the hum of the overhead lights, and I just couldn't keep my focus locked on what was right in front of me. 

And honestly, it's the exact same feeling I get now at work with this new system. It's just this inability to stay locked onto something if I'm just reading it instead of doing it. Like, I can start a digital work order thinking I’ve got it, but halfway through reading the notes my mind slips off to the next noise or job and I realize I don’t know what I just looked at. I'll hear a dog barking three floors down, or a truck backing up in the alley, or I'll start thinking about a drywall patch I need to sand in unit 2C, and suddenly I'm just staring at this heavy black tablet like it's written in a foreign language. I have to read the exact same sentence three or four times because my focus just completely evaporates. 

So, yeah, people have been telling me I have trouble paying attention my whole entire life. If I have to just sit and sustain my focus on words or instructions, whether it was a textbook back in the day or Dave's digital tickets now, my brain just... goes on vacation.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.8 (other mental disorders due to known physiological condition) - no head injury, illness, or medical event 11 months ago. Ruled out F07.9 (unspecified personality and behavioral disorder due to disease, injury, or dysfunction of brain) - same reasoning. Ruled out F32.9 (major depressive disorder) - patient denies mood symptoms, maintains interest in activities and relationships. Strong confirmation of F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified): lifelong history of inattention and distractibility since grade school, difficulty sustaining focus on written/verbal information, easily distracted by environmental stimuli, loses papers and forgets instructions, but intact procedural/working memory for hands-on tasks. Recent worsening is due to environmental mismatch (shift from physical paper tickets to abstract digital system requiring sustained attention), not new pathology.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the clinic
opening_question.question: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been going on that made you decide to come see me?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, distractibility, and forgetfulness dating back to childhood (third grade), with reports from teachers and family of being 'easily distracted,' 'off in the clouds,' and unable to sustain focus on written tasks. While symptoms acutely worsened 11 months ago due to occupational stress (transition to digital work orders), the core presentation is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive type. The patient demonstrates intact procedural memory and motor skills (can perform complex repairs without difficulty), preserved orientation and basic cognitive function, and no evidence of confusion, mood disorder, or acquired brain injury. The functional impairment at work (missed appointments, dropped tasks, poor digital task completion) directly results from attentional deficits rather than depression or anxiety. The recent exacerbation reflects poor fit between his lifelong attentional profile and new environmental demands, not new-onset cognitive decline.
